segments.text: One of the best things about talking to tools like chat, GPT, Claude, or Gemini, is how incredibly polite they are.
The replies are usually friendly, positive, and deeply encouraging.
But that programmed enthusiasm becomes a problem when you genuinely need honest criticism.
Treating an AI's cheerful approval as an objective evaluation is a mistake.
Let's call it the flattery trap.
Take a look at this comparison board.
At the top, we ask an AI to evaluate a very basic introduction for an essay on the Great Gatsby.
The student writes that people have thought about the American dream, some achieve it, some don't, and Fitzgerald explores the idea.
The response on the left falls right into the flattery trap.
It says, great start, you've clearly identified the central theme. This is a strong foundation.
That praise is empty.
It could fit almost any Gatsby essay, evaluating the writing without pointing to a single line
that actually earned the compliment.
Now look at the useful feedback on the right.
Here, the AI identifies exactly what the writing lacks.
It notes that the topic is there, but asks, what does Gatsby's experience suggest about that dream?
It then prescribes a specific next step, right at thesis that says what Fitzgerald actually shows.
Actionable feedback gives you a roadmap to improve the work.
Empty praise only improves how you feel about the draft you already have.
After you spend hours writing an essay or drafting a plan, human nature makes great start
sound much better than a list of missing elements.
The developers who train these tools know that.
The AI's preference for cheering you on is a direct result of how it learns from human feedback,
specifically a training mechanism called reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF.
This diagram shows how praise gets baked in.
First, human reviewers rank AI answers.
Step 2 highlights the flaw.
Reviewers frequently choose the answer offering praise, rewarding validation over critical breakdowns.
Finally, the training model adjusts to those preferences, permanently locking flattery into its baseline behavior.
Taking to its extreme, this training loop creates psychofancy, excessive, unearned agreement.
To see how far this goes, a user recently pitched chat GPT a completely absurd gag product.
A fake item will politely call poop on a stick just to see if the AI would push back.
Here is the text of the AI's response.
It calls the terrible idea absolutely brilliant and claims it taps perfectly into the energy of the current cultural moment.
It validates a terrible joke as genius and performance art with the potential to explode.
While companies attempt to patch and test for this extreme level of agreement,
the underlying bias toward validation remains embedded in the tool.
To get real analysis, you have to actively override it.
To bypass the trap, give the AI a rigid standard so it cannot default to agreeing with you.
Move 1 is to share your opinion last.
A weak prompt says, I think this plan is good.
Thoughts?
The better prompt asks, evaluate this plan before I tell you what I think.
If you announce your confidence upfront, the AI's psychofancy protocol will likely validate your feelings.
With holding your verdict, forces it to audit the work itself.
Move 2 is to explicitly ask for the gaps.
Instead of a broad question like, is my essay good?
You instruct the AI to find what is weak, what is missing, and what a critic would say.
Asking if something is good invites a cheerful yes.
Asking for the gaps commands the AI to hunt for specific structural flaws.
Move 3 is the most rigorous tactic.
Force it to use a rubric.
Instead of a generic request to grade my essay, you provide a specific standard.
You tell it to grade against your supplied rubric, quote, exact evidence from your text,
and explain how to move up one level.
This eliminates arbitrary praise and demands a precise roadmap for the next draft.
If your platform supports it, you can automate this by setting a standing instruction.
You can command the system to always be direct, lead with what needs work, and point to specific evidence.
Overriding the flattery trap takes a deliberate shift in how you prompt.
Your goal is to command the machine to improve your material, not to seek emotional validation for your effort.
Left to its own devices, AI will learn to tell you exactly what you want to hear.
It is entirely up to you to steer the machine away from comfort and toward feedback you can actually use.
